RNA Viruses I
Microbiology LE 2 · Interactive lecture reviewer

Overview

A whole-lecture orientation only. The lesson proper begins in the next tab. This lecture compares major human Picornaviruses, Reoviridae, and Caliciviridae, with emphasis on structure, replication, disease patterns, diagnosis, prevention, and high-yield distinguishing features.

Main framework p. 1

GroupGenome and envelopeMajor lecture membersMajor disease anchors
PicornaviridaeSingle-stranded, positive-sense RNA. Non-enveloped.Enteroviruses, Poliovirus, Coxsackievirus, Echoviruses, Rhinoviruses, Hepatitis A virus, ParechovirusPoliomyelitis, aseptic meningitis, myocarditis, mucocutaneous disease, common cold, acute Hepatitis A, neonatal sepsis-like illness
ReoviridaeDouble-stranded RNA. Segmented. Non-enveloped.Rotavirus is the main human pathogen emphasized.Infantile gastroenteritis with malabsorption and secretory diarrhea
CaliciviridaeSingle-stranded, positive-sense RNA. Non-segmented. Non-enveloped.Norovirus and SapovirusEpidemic viral gastroenteritis, especially Norovirus outbreaks

High-yield orientation

Picornavirus pattern

Small, positive-sense ssRNA, non-enveloped. A broad clinical spectrum occurs because different members have distinct tissue tropisms.

Reovirus pattern

Segmented dsRNA permits reassortment and therefore genetic shift. Rotavirus has an 11-segment genome.

Calicivirus pattern

Cup-shaped capsid depressions and a single major structural protein are lecture-marked structural clues.
Must-know anchors
Rhinovirus is the common cold virus.
Rotavirus Group A is the most common human rotavirus pathogen.
Norovirus is the most common cause of nonbacterial gastroenteritis worldwide.
HAV has no chronic carrier state.

Picornaviridae Foundations

Core family-level structure, genome, tropism, clinical spectrum, and replication. These features explain the later virus-specific patterns.

Identity and classification p. 1 p. 2

  • “Pico” means small and “rna” refers to the RNA genome.
  • The lecture calls Picornaviruses the smallest RNA viruses. They have tiny virions and simple genomes but are very diverse.
  • Family Picornaviridae contains 12 genera in the lecture classification.
  • Core property: single-stranded, positive-sense, non-enveloped RNA virus.
  • The lecture states that this core property is shared with Caliciviridae, so the two families can behave in similar ways.
Human groupWhere the lecture says it replicatesMain disease anchor
EnterovirusesGut and throatSystemic diseases including polio, Coxsackievirus disease, and Echovirus disease
RhinovirusesNose and throatUpper respiratory tract infection and common cold
HepatovirusLiverAcute Hepatitis A
ParechovirusRespiratory and gastrointestinal tractsMild respiratory or GI disease, meningitis, and neonatal sepsis-like illness
Taxonomy note
Rhinoviruses are now placed within the Enterovirus genus by ICTV taxonomy in the lecture.
Clinically and traditionally, the lecture still separates Rhinoviruses because their properties differ from other Enteroviruses.
Parechovirus types 1 and 2 were formerly Echoviruses 22 and 23.

Clinical spectrum p. 2

  • Picornavirus disease can affect many organs.
  • Poliomyelitis is the most serious Enterovirus disease listed.
  • Other syndromes include aseptic meningitis, myocarditis, pleurodynia, conjunctivitis, skin and mucosal lesions, febrile illness, and respiratory infections.
  • Subclinical infection is more common than overt disease. Most patients are asymptomatic. Symptomatic disease is often mild.
  • Clinical diagnosis can be difficult because the same virus can cause multiple syndromes and different viruses can cause similar syndromes.

Capsid and genome p. 2

  • The capsid protects the genome and has 60 subunits.
  • Each repeating unit contains VP1, VP2, VP3, and VP4.
  • VP1 to VP3 are surface proteins. VP4 is internal.
  • Capsid symmetry is icosahedral.
  • The genome is the infectious portion of the virus and is single-stranded, positive-sense, nonsegmented RNA of about 7 to 8 kb.
  • The 5′ end has VPg, which serves as a primer or starting point for RNA synthesis.
  • The 3′ poly-A tail contributes to RNA stability.
  • There is no envelope.
Genome behavior
The lecture emphasizes that nonsegmented RNA does not undergo genetic shift.
Mutation usually produces genetic drift.
By contrast, segmented RNA viruses can mix genome segments and undergo a sudden change called genetic shift.

The canyon and receptor binding p. 2 p. 3

  • The junction of VP1, VP2, and VP3 creates a surface canyon.
  • The receptor-binding site lies protected within the canyon.
  • The lecture states that the canyon is too narrow for antibody penetration but can admit host-cell receptors.
  • Binding at this site attaches the virion to its host cell.

Replication cycle p. 3

1. Attachment to host-cell receptor. Receptor identity determines tropism.
↓
2. Uncoating after receptor-induced conformational change. RNA is released into the cytoplasm.
↓
3. Translation of positive-sense RNA directly into a single polyprotein.
↓
4. Processing by viral protease into structural proteins and replication proteins.
↓
5. RNA replication by viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. A negative-sense strand is made and used as template for many positive-sense strands.
↓
6. Assembly and maturation. Positive strands are encapsidated. VP0 is cleaved into VP2 and VP4 to complete the capsid.
↓
7. Release of virions by host-cell lysis.
Receptor anchors
Poliovirus host-cell receptor: PVR.
Coxsackievirus B host-cell receptor: CAR.
Echovirus host-cell receptor: DAF.
The cycle is rapid at about 5 to 10 hours.

Enterovirus

General physical characteristics, pathogenesis, mutation, and immunity before the lecture separates Poliovirus, Coxsackievirus, and Echovirus.

Why “Entero” p. 3

Key differentiator
Entero refers to the gut or intestine because these viruses replicate in the gastrointestinal tract.
The lecture emphasizes that Enteroviruses barely cause gastrointestinal symptoms despite the name.

Physical characteristics

  • Stable over a wide pH range of 3 to 10.
  • Acid stable, allowing survival through the stomach and entry into the GI tract.
  • Replicate at about 37°C.
  • No lipid envelope, making them resistant to ether, chloroform, and alcohol.
  • Inactivated by radiation, formaldehyde, and phenol.
  • The lecture highlights formaldehyde because it is used to create killed vaccines.
  • MgCl₂ reduces thermolability and can help produce vaccines that do not require refrigeration.

Pathogenesis p. 4

Entry by fecal-oral or respiratory route
↓
Initial replication in the pharynx and distal small bowel, especially Peyer’s patches
↓
Lymph-node spread
↓
Minor viremia with no symptoms
↓
Major viremia if replication is not contained
↓
Organ dissemination to sites such as CNS, heart, and skin
  • Most infections remain subclinical.
  • Disease expression depends on host factors such as immunity, nutrition, and pregnancy.
  • The lecture describes major viremia as producing a minor constitutional illness with fever, malaise, and vomiting.

Mutation and evolution p. 4

  • RNA replication has a high error rate, about one error per genome replication in the lecture.
  • This contributes to genetic drift and to vaccine-derived polioviruses.
  • Recombination can occur during co-infection with different strains.
  • The lecture mechanism: if two strains replicate in the same cell, the polymerase can jump from one template to another, producing a recombinant genome.
Must Know — Recombination
Multiple viral strains can replicate in the same cell.
The polymerase may switch templates during replication.
This can create a recombinant genome and cause mutation.

Immunity p. 4

  • Immunity is serotype-specific.
  • Neutralizing IgG persists for life.
  • IgM appears early.
  • IgA protects mucosal surfaces in the GI tract.
  • Maternal antibodies protect infants through the placenta and breast milk.
  • B-cell deficient patients cannot produce antibodies and can develop persistent infections.
  • T cells and macrophages help clear infection, but T-cell activity can also contribute to immunopathology by damaging healthy cells.

Poliovirus

Neurotropic Enterovirus causing acute CNS disease with characteristic lower-motor-neuron injury and asymmetric flaccid paralysis.

Core identity p. 4

  • Genus Enterovirus, family Picornaviridae.
  • Three antigenic types: Types 1 to 3. The lecture states that Type 1 is the most common cause of paralysis.
  • Small, non-enveloped, positive-sense RNA virus.
  • Acid stable and resistant to ether.
  • Inactivated by 55°C for 30 minutes and by chlorine.
  • Humans are the only natural reservoir in the lecture.
  • Infection requires the primate-specific CD155 or PVR receptor. Absence of the receptor confers resistance to infection.
What poliomyelitis means
Polio refers to gray matter.
Myelo refers to the spinal cord in medical usage.
Itis means inflammation.
Poliomyelitis therefore means inflammation of the gray matter of the spinal cord.

Neurotropism and flaccid paralysis p. 4

  • Poliovirus causes acute infection and inflammation of the CNS.
  • It destroys anterior motor neurons of the spinal cord.
  • The resulting lower-motor-neuron syndrome is flaccid paralysis.
  • Flaccid paralysis features loss of voluntary movement, hypotonia, reduced or absent reflexes, and asymmetric weakness.
Do not confuse the target
Poliovirus multiplies in nerve cells and causes cytolysis.
It does not multiply in muscle.
Muscle damage and atrophy are secondary to denervation from lower-motor-neuron injury.

Pathogenesis p. 4 p. 5

Mouth and ingestion of fecally contaminated food or water
↓
Oropharynx and intestine, including tonsils and Peyer’s patches
↓
Bloodstream
↓
CNS invasion through blood or peripheral nerves
↓
Motor neurons in spinal cord and brainstem
↓
Cytolysis and motor-neuron loss
↓
Virus shedding in stool for weeks
  • Virus can reach the spinal cord and brain through blood or along axons of peripheral nerves.
  • Other lecture-associated pathology includes myocarditis, lymphatic hyperplasia, and ulceration of Peyer’s patches.
  • Incubation is about 7 to 14 days.
  • Virus can be detected in throat and stool before illness. Stool shedding can continue for weeks.
  • Antibodies appear before paralysis.

Clinical spectrum p. 5

Subclinical infection

  • More than 90% of infections are subclinical or asymptomatic.

Mild disease

  • The most common symptomatic form in the lecture.
  • Febrile illness, sore throat, GI upset, malaise, drowsiness, headache, nausea, vomiting, and constipation.
  • Complete recovery usually occurs within a few days.

Nonparalytic poliomyelitis

  • Produces aseptic meningitis with neck and back stiffness.
  • Nuchal rigidity is stiffness and pain when the neck is flexed forward due to meningeal and spinal-root irritation.
  • May include headache and mental-status changes.
  • There is no significant destruction of anterior horn neurons.
  • Complete recovery occurs in about 2 to 10 days.

Paralytic poliomyelitis

  • Rare compared with nonparalytic disease.
  • Produces asymmetric flaccid paralysis, commonly of the lower limbs.
  • Residual deficits are common.
  • Brainstem invasion can cause incoordination.
  • Painful spasms may occur in nonparalyzed muscles.
  • There are no sensory deficits because the lecture localizes damage to the anterior horn.
  • Most recover within six months, although some do not recover fully.
Bulbar poliomyelitis
Infection involves the medulla oblongata.
Motor nerves involved in the lecture include the phrenic nerve, intercostal nerves, and cranial nerves IX, X, and XII.
Consequences include impaired diaphragmatic or intercostal movement, swallowing difficulty, loss of airway protection, and respiratory paralysis.
Severe respiratory paralysis may require ventilatory support.

Postpoliomyelitis syndrome p. 5

  • A late return of weakness decades after paralytic poliomyelitis.
  • The lecture estimates it in about 20 to 30% of patients who had paralytic disease.
  • New muscle weakness, pain, atrophy, and fatigue may appear 25 to 35 years after the acute illness.
  • It is not caused by reactivation of poliovirus.
  • Recovery from the original injury depends partly on surviving neurons sprouting new axonal branches.
  • These small branches are unstable and metabolically demanding. With aging, support can fail and symptoms return.

Diagnosis p. 5 p. 6

ComponentLecture details
SpecimensThroat swab early. Stool has the longest yield. Poliovirus is rarely recovered from CSF.
Gold standardCell culture with cytopathic effect after about 3 to 6 days.
RT-PCRRapid, sensitive, and specific.
SerologyRise in antibody titer. Less sensitive than PCR.
NeutralizationConfirmatory after culture. Specific antiserum prevents cytopathic effect if it neutralizes the virus.
MRICan demonstrate anterior horn involvement.

CSF pattern of aseptic viral meningitis

  • Increased white cells with lymphocytic predominance.
  • Protein can be increased or normal.
  • Glucose is normal.

Immunity and epidemiology p. 6

  • Immunity is type-specific and lifelong, mainly through humoral neutralizing antibodies.
  • Cross-protection is limited.
  • Maternal antibody protects infants for up to about 6 months.
  • High blood antibody levels do not affect virus already in the brain. The lecture therefore emphasizes immunization before nervous-system symptoms.
  • Before vaccines, the lecture cites about 21,000 paralytic cases per year in the United States.
  • Transmission occurs by fecal-oral route, pharyngeal secretions, and contaminated water.
  • Children are usually more susceptible than adults because adults often have acquired immunity.
  • Risk rises with poor sanitation and crowding.
  • The lecture notes year-round occurrence in the tropics and summer or fall peaks in temperate regions.
Lecture epidemiology wording
One epidemiology section lists Afghanistan, Pakistan, and Nigeria as countries remaining polio-endemic.
A later global-eradication section describes remaining endemic areas as Afghanistan, Pakistan, and parts of Africa.
This reviewer preserves the lecture statements without replacing them with outside updates.

Vaccination and control p. 6 p. 7

Main vaccine difference
IPV or Salk protects against CNS disease but does not create local intestinal immunity.
OPV or Sabin creates systemic and mucosal immunity and can interrupt transmission.
The lecture’s key differentiator is that OPV induces gut immunity.
FeatureIPV — SalkOPV — Sabin
VirusInactivated or killedLive attenuated
RouteInjectedOral
ImmunityHumoral antibodiesIgG, IgM, and IgA in the gut
Gut infectionDoes not induce local intestinal immunity. Virus can still multiply in the gut.Gut becomes more resistant because vaccine virus multiplies in the intestine.
Community effectDoes not immunize unvaccinated contacts.Vaccine progeny can be shed in stool and may expose unvaccinated contacts, producing community immunity in the lecture explanation.
Major limitationNo local gut immunity.Oral vaccine interference, vaccine-derived poliovirus, and rare vaccine-associated paralysis.
  • Vaccination is the only effective method of preventing poliomyelitis in the lecture.
  • There is no antiviral therapy.
  • OPV immunity may be blocked if another Enterovirus infection is present during vaccination.
  • The lecture cites a rare vaccine-associated paralytic case at about 1 per 2 million vaccinated persons.
  • Mnemonic from the lecture: SALK = killed virus. SABIN = oral live virus.

Global eradication and Philippine notes p. 6 p. 7

  • WHO campaign began in 1988. The lecture states cases dropped from about 350,000 to fewer than 2,000 per year.
  • Polio-free regions listed: Americas in 1994, Western Pacific in 2000, and Europe in 2002.
  • Wild poliovirus type 2 is described as eradicated, with the last case in 1999.
  • The Philippines was declared polio-free in 2000.
  • A 2019 outbreak was linked to circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus.
  • Cases were detected in Mindanao, NCR, and some parts of Luzon.
  • The lecture states that no new confirmed cases occurred since 2020 and surveillance continued.
  • Sabayang Patak Kontra Polio was a synchronized national OPV campaign in response to the outbreak and detection of polioviruses in NCR waterways.
  • Mass administration targeted children below 5 years regardless of vaccination status.
  • For children under 1 year, the lecture lists three OPV doses and two IPV doses in routine immunization.

Treatment p. 7

  • No antiviral drug is available for poliovirus infection.
  • Management is supportive and symptomatic.
  • The lecture states that quarantine is ineffective because subclinical infection is common.

Coxsackievirus

Enteroviruses separated historically into Group A and Group B by their effects in inoculated mice, with distinct high-yield clinical patterns.

General features p. 7

  • Genus Enterovirus, family Picornaviridae. More common than polio in the lecture.
  • Single-stranded, positive-sense RNA and non-enveloped.
  • Groups A, B, and C are listed, but the lecture discusses A and B.
  • Historical mouse distinction: Group A caused flaccid paralysis. Group B caused spastic paralysis.
  • Spastic paralysis is linked to UMN injury with hypertonia and hyperreflexia.
  • Transmission is fecal-oral and respiratory. Contact with bodily fluids can be direct or indirect.
  • Virus can be recovered from blood early, throat early, and stool for 5 to 6 weeks.
  • Many infections are subclinical.
Lecture memory aid
Type A = Above the neck: oral ulcers, conjunctivitis, rashes.
Type B = Below the neck or Body organs: heart, chest, and systemic illness.

Clinical spectrum p. 7 p. 8

GroupMajor lecture syndromes
Coxsackie AHerpangina
Hand-foot-and-mouth disease
Acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis, especially A24 variant
Coxsackie BPleurodynia or Bornholm disease
Myocarditis and pericarditis
Severe neonatal systemic disease involving heart, liver, and brain
BothFebrile illness
Respiratory infection
Meningoencephalitis
Non-polio paralysis that is incomplete and reversible
Aseptic meningitis

Incubation is about 2 to 9 days.

Coxsackie A p. 7 p. 8

Herpangina

  • Severe febrile pharyngitis with abrupt fever and sore throat.
  • Discrete vesicles appear on the posterior half of the palate, pharynx, tonsils, or tongue.
  • Lecture contrast: streptococcal pharyngitis produces exudative tonsillitis with white or yellow pus rather than an ulcer.

Hand-foot-and-mouth disease

  • Commonly caused by Coxsackie A16, although other strains can cause it.
  • Common in children, schools, and daycares. Adults can also be affected.
  • Prodrome 24 to 48 hours before the main symptoms: fever, sore throat, and malaise.
  • Rash involves hands, feet, and mouth and lasts about 5 to 10 days.
  • Oral and pharyngeal ulcerations occur.
  • Vesicular rash occurs on palms and soles and can spread to arms and legs.
  • The vesicles heal without crusting, unlike herpesvirus and poxvirus lesions in the lecture comparison.

Acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis

  • Caused by Coxsackievirus A24 variant. The lecture notes Enterovirus 70 as the classic cause.
  • Highly contagious.
  • Virus infects conjunctival epithelium.
  • Produces subconjunctival hemorrhage, edema, and intense inflammation.
  • Self-limited in about 5 to 7 days.
Coxsackie A “Triple H”
Hand-foot-and-mouth disease.
Herpangina.
Acute Hemorrhagic conjunctivitis.

Coxsackie B p. 8

Pleurodynia or Bornholm disease

  • Fever with stabbing chest pain.
  • Usually abrupt in onset.
  • May be preceded by malaise, headache, and anorexia.
  • Self-limited from about two days to two weeks. Recovery is complete, although relapse can occur.

Acute myocarditis

  • Acute inflammation of heart muscle.
  • Coxsackie B is the most common type listed.
  • Can be fatal in neonates and can cause permanent heart damage.
  • Virus enters myocytes through receptors such as CAR, the coxsackievirus and adenovirus receptor.
  • The lecture also lists adenovirus, coronavirus, parvovirus B19, HCV, EBV, other Enteroviruses, and HHV-6 as viral causes of acute myocarditis.

Generalized disease of infants

  • Simultaneous viral infection of multiple organs including heart, liver, and brain.
  • May be fatal or may resolve.
  • Can sometimes be acquired transplacentally.

Diagnosis, epidemiology, and control p. 8

  • Collect specimens according to the site of disease.
  • Possible samples: throat swab early, stool for weeks, vesicular fluid, conjunctival swab, and CSF in aseptic meningitis.
  • Methods: cell culture with cytopathic effect in 5 to 14 days, RT-PCR, and type-specific neutralizing antibody serology.
  • Worldwide distribution. Virus can be found in sewage, water, and feces.
  • Summer and early-fall peaks are described.
  • Children are frequently infected and can bring infection home to family members.
  • Familial and close-contact spread is common.
  • No vaccine or antiviral is available. Prevention relies on hygiene and sanitation. Care is supportive.

Hepatitis A Virus

A hepatotropic Picornavirus causing acute, self-limited hepatitis without chronic carriage.

General features p. 8

  • Family Picornaviridae, genus Hepatovirus.
  • Small, non-enveloped, icosahedral, positive-sense ssRNA virus of about 27 to 32 nm.
  • Three genotypes infect humans: I, II, and III.
  • One serotype produces lifelong immunity after infection.
  • Environmentally stable. Resistant to acid at about pH 3, ether, and moderate heat.
  • More heat stable than other Picornaviruses in the lecture.
  • Inactivated by hypochlorite bleach and quaternary ammonium formulations containing HC as stated in the lecture.

Transmission and epidemiology p. 8 p. 9

  • Fecal-oral transmission through contaminated food, water, or close contact.
  • Outbreak settings include daycares, camps, schools, military settings, and nursing homes.
  • Risk groups listed: travelers, men who have sex with men, drug users, patients with clotting-factor disorders, and patients with chronic liver disease.
  • For clotting-factor disorders, the lecture notes use of plasma-derived concentrates and states that Hepatitis A can remain stable in these products.
Major sources
Raw or undercooked shellfish.
Contaminated food and water.
The lecture explains that clams and oysters can filter contaminated water and become infected.

Enterohepatic cycling p. 9

Ingestion of infected material
↓
Stomach passage because HAV is acid resistant
↓
Lower intestine replication
↓
Liver transport, the major replication site
↓
Release from infected liver cells into sinusoids and canaliculi
↓
Bile and intestine
↓
Fecal excretion and fecal-oral spread

The lecture notes that HAV resembles other hepatitis viruses in targeting the liver but is not genetically related to the other hepatitis viruses.

Pathogenesis p. 9

The virus is not the main direct killer
HAV is not directly cytopathic in the usual course.
The main cause of hepatocyte injury is the immune response to infected cells.
At peak replication, many hepatocytes can contain HAV antigen without widespread necrosis.
  • As adaptive immunity develops, liver damage becomes apparent.
  • CD8+ T cells are cytotoxic against HAV-infected cells.
  • NK cells can lyse HAV-infected cells.
  • Antibodies from B cells mainly help limit viral spread rather than drive pathology.

Clinical features p. 9

  • Incubation is about 4 weeks.
  • Acute inflammatory liver disease with fever, malaise, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, and icteric sclerae.
  • Loss of appetite and weight loss are common.
  • Dark urine is described as a common first sign prompting consultation.
  • Stool can become pale or clay colored.
  • Disease is self-limited. By the third week, most patients feel better.
  • Children younger than 5 years are often asymptomatic.
  • Adults are more likely to have symptoms and jaundice. Symptomatic disease increases with age.
No chronic disease
There is no chronic infection and no cirrhosis from HAV in the lecture.
This is used to distinguish HAV from Hepatitis B and C.

Complications

  • Fulminant hepatitis is rare and is higher risk in people who already have chronic liver disease.
  • Fulminant disease can produce rapid loss of liver function with encephalopathy and coagulopathy.
  • Cholestatic hepatitis: fever, pruritus, and prolonged jaundice.
  • Relapsing Hepatitis A is very rare and may be fatal.
  • Rare autoimmune triggering can include autoimmune hepatitis or extrahepatic autoimmune disease.
  • Rare extrahepatic manifestations listed include cholecystitis, acute pancreatitis, interstitial hepatitis, postviral encephalitis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome.
  • Most cases are benign and self-limited. Severe or fatal disease is uncommon and is more likely in older patients.
  • Long-term sequelae are not observed after recovery in the lecture.

Laboratory diagnosis p. 9

  • HAV cannot be clinically distinguished reliably from other causes of hepatitis.
  • Virus can be detected in stool from about 2 weeks before to 2 weeks after jaundice.
  • IgM anti-HAV indicates acute infection. It appears early and lasts about 3 to 6 months.
  • IgG anti-HAV with negative IgM indicates prior infection or vaccination.
  • ELISA is the test of choice in the lecture.
  • AST and ALT can indicate parenchymal liver damage but are nonspecific.

Prevention, vaccination, and treatment p. 10

  • Inactivated HAV vaccine is safe and effective.
  • Recommended for all children older than 1 year and for high-risk groups listed in the lecture.
  • Immunoglobulin can be used for post-exposure prophylaxis within 2 weeks.
  • Prevention includes handwashing, safe food and water, and chlorine disinfection.
  • The lecture states that Hepatitis A vaccine is not part of the Philippine National Immunization Program but is recommended from age 1 year and up.
  • Treatment is supportive only. Prevent dehydration, maintain nutrition, and rest.
  • Fulminant cases require appropriate management and may require liver transplantation.
Lecture mnemonics
A = Acute.
A = Anus to mouth.
HAV = Hand washing avoids virus.
A = Adolescents Abroad for travel risk.
A = No afterlife to recall usually benign disease with no chronic disease and no cancer in the lecture mnemonic.

Echoviruses

Historically “orphan” Enteroviruses that were first isolated from humans before specific disease associations became established.

Name and general features p. 10

  • ECHO = Enteric Cytopathogenic Human Orphan Viruses.
  • Family Picornaviridae, genus Enterovirus.
  • Single-stranded, positive-sense RNA.
  • The lecture lists 30 serotypes, not all linked to disease.
  • Transmission and epidemiology are similar to Coxsackievirus.
Part of ECHOLecture explanation
EntericFirst isolated from the gastrointestinal tract in stool. Spreads by fecal-oral route.
CytopathogenicProduced cytopathic effects in cell culture, with infected cells dying or changing structure.
HumanIsolated from humans rather than animals.
OrphanWhen discovered in the 1950s, the viruses had no known parent disease association.

Later associations included aseptic meningitis, respiratory illness, conjunctivitis, and rashes.

Clinical syndromes p. 10

  • Clinical syndromes resemble Coxsackievirus disease.
  • Aseptic meningitis is common, especially in summer outbreaks.
  • Encephalitis and febrile illnesses can occur and may include rash.
  • Rash is noted particularly in young children.
  • Infantile diarrhea has a possible association, but the lecture states it is unproven.
  • Enterovirus 70 causes acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis with sudden painful red eye and subconjunctival hemorrhage, resolving in about 10 days.
  • Enterovirus 71 is a major cause of CNS disease, including meningitis, encephalitis, and polio-like paralysis, and is associated with severe or fatal hand-foot-and-mouth disease outbreaks.

Diagnosis and epidemiology p. 10 p. 11

  • Clinical diagnosis is unreliable because symptoms overlap with other Enteroviruses.
  • Suspicion rises during summer meningitis outbreaks or summer epidemics of febrile rash in children.
  • PCR is rapid and sensitive.
  • Virus can be isolated from throat, stool, or CSF.
  • Serology is impractical because there are many types.
  • Mixed infection with multiple Enteroviruses can occur.
  • Worldwide distribution, particularly among children younger than 1 year.
  • Summer-autumn seasonality and higher incidence in lower socioeconomic groups are described.
  • Family clusters and rapid spread are common.

Prevention and recall cues p. 11

  • No vaccine or antiviral is available.
  • The lecture states that infection generally leads to complete recovery.
  • Prevention uses general hygiene and avoidance of exposing infants or children to febrile cases.
Lecture tip
Think of Coxsackie and Summer when recalling Echoviruses.
Enterovirus 70 → acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis.
Enterovirus 71 → CNS disease and hand-foot-and-mouth disease.

Rhinoviruses

The lecture’s classic common-cold virus, separated clinically from other Enteroviruses by acid lability and preferred growth in the cooler nasopharynx.

General features p. 11

Classic association
Rhinovirus = common cold virus.
It is the most common cause of mild upper respiratory tract infections in the lecture.
  • Positive-sense, non-enveloped ssRNA virus in Picornaviridae.
  • The lecture lists approximately 150+ serotypes.
  • There is no cross-protective immunity.
  • Acid labile and inactivated below pH 5 to 6.
  • Acid lability prevents survival in the stomach and helps explain why Rhinovirus does not replicate in the intestine.
  • Optimal growth at about 33°C, the nasopharyngeal temperature in the lecture.
  • Replication is limited above this temperature, supporting its upper-airway tropism.
  • Thermostable enough to survive for hours on surfaces.
Do not confuse
Enteroviruses are acid stable and can reach the intestine.
Rhinoviruses are acid labile and instead grow in the nasopharynx.
Must Know — Other causes of URTI
Coronaviruses.
Adenoviruses.
Enteroviruses.
Parainfluenza viruses.
Influenza viruses.

Receptors and pathogenesis p. 11

  • Major receptor groups use ICAM-1.
  • Minor receptor groups use the LDLR family.
  • Entry is through the upper respiratory tract.
  • Replication is limited mainly to nasal mucosal epithelium.
  • Symptoms correlate with viral load in nasal secretions.
  • Benign disease shows little histopathology. The lecture lists edema, mild inflammation, and increased nasal secretions.
  • Rhinovirus rarely causes lower respiratory tract disease but is a major trigger of asthma exacerbations.

Common-cold misconception p. 11

Lecture misconception
Wearing wet clothes or being drenched in water does not directly produce a cold and does not directly increase susceptibility to the virus.
Transmission is mainly by direct contact and respiratory droplets.
The lecture explanation is that rainy conditions may keep people indoors in closer contact, increasing opportunities for viral spread.

Clinical findings p. 11 p. 12

  • Incubation: 2 to 4 days.
  • Typical duration: about 7 days. Cough may persist for 2 to 3 weeks.
  • Sneezing, nasal congestion, nasal discharge, sore throat, mild cough, malaise, and chilly sensation.
  • Fever is uncommon. The lecture cue is chills rather than fever.
  • Clinical findings are not sufficiently distinct to separate Rhinovirus from other viral colds. Specific diagnosis requires laboratory testing.
  • Children can develop otitis media, sinusitis, bronchitis, and pneumonitis.
  • The lecture mechanism for secondary bacterial complications is mucus stasis, which allows bacteria to proliferate when drainage is blocked.

Immunity, epidemiology, diagnosis, and control p. 12

  • Neutralizing antibodies in serum and secretions develop about 7 to 21 days after infection.
  • The lecture stresses that recovery does not depend on neutralizing antibodies because they may appear after recovery.
  • Protection is type-specific and short-lived. Serum antibody can persist while titers decline.
  • Antibody may contribute to final viral clearance.
  • Reinfection with new serotypes is common. The lecture notes about two infections per year in adults.
  • Worldwide distribution across all ages.
  • Fall and spring peaks are described in temperate zones.
  • Transmission occurs by hand-to-hand contact, hand-to-eye contact, contaminated objects, and respiratory spread. The lecture states self-inoculation is more important than airborne spread.
  • Highest rates occur in children, who can introduce infection into families.
  • PCR is the best specific diagnostic test but is rarely useful for patient management because disease is usually benign.
  • No vaccine because of many serotypes and short-lived immunity.
  • No specific antiviral is available in the lecture.
  • Prevention relies on hand hygiene and avoiding contact with sick individuals.
Interferon-α lecture point
Intranasal interferon-α has been shown experimentally to reduce family spread.
The lecture explanation is that it warns host cells, induces an antiviral state, and blocks viral RNA replication and protein synthesis.

Parechovirus

A divergent Picornavirus genus with an especially important neonatal sepsis-like presentation.

Structure and classification p. 12

  • Genus defined in the 1990s.
  • The lecture lists 14 types.
  • Types 1 and 2 were formerly Echoviruses 22 and 23.
  • Divergent from Enteroviruses, with less than 30% protein-sequence identity in the lecture.
  • Capsid has only three proteins because VP0 is not cleaved.
  • Transmission and replication involve the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts.

Clinical features p. 12

  • Mild GI illness.
  • Mild respiratory illness.
  • Meningitis.
  • Neonatal sepsis-like illness.
Red, Angry Baby Virus
Fever.
Irritability.
Diffuse reddish rash.
Sepsis-like presentation.

Epidemiology and detection p. 13

  • Common in early childhood.
  • Human parechovirus 1 was among the top 15 Enterovirus detections from 2006 to 2008 in the lecture.
  • Likely underreported because routine Enterovirus PCR assays may not detect it.

Reoviridae

A fundamentally different RNA-virus strategy: double-stranded, segmented genomes packaged with enzymes needed to transcribe viral mRNA.

Name and general features p. 13

  • Lecture mnemonic: R = Respiratory, E = Enteric, O = Orphan.
  • Medium-sized, double-stranded RNA, segmented, icosahedral viruses.
  • Genome contains about 10 to 12 segments depending on genus.
  • Non-enveloped.
  • Includes Rotavirus, Orthoreovirus, Coltivirus, and Orbivirus.
Double-stranded RNA
The genome has both negative and positive RNA strands.
A special polymerase is required to transcribe mRNA from the genome.
Segmented RNA
The genome is split into multiple separate RNA molecules.
Segments from two strains can reassort in a co-infected cell.
The resulting genomic reassortment can produce genetic shift.

Structure p. 13

  • Virion size: about 60 to 80 nm.
  • The core contains enzymes for transcription and RNA capping.
  • Rotavirus has a lecture-marked triple-layered capsid.
  • Rotavirus is stable to heat at 50°C, pH 3 to 9, and lipid solvents as stated in the lecture.
  • It is inactivated by ethanol, phenol, and chlorine.
  • Proteolytic cleavage increases infectivity.
GenusGenome segments
Rotavirus11
Orthoreovirus10
Orbivirus10
Coltivirus12

Classification p. 13

  • Two subfamilies in the lecture.
  • Spinareovirinae: spiked inner capsid. Includes Orthoreovirus.
  • Sedoreovirinae: smooth inner capsid. Includes Rotavirus.
  • Rotavirus groups A to E are listed, with tentative F and G.
  • Human disease is associated with Groups A, B, and C.

Rotavirus replication cycle p. 13

1. Attachment: VP4 spike protein binds host-cell receptors.
↓
2. Partial uncoating in lysosomes: outer VP4 and VP7 shell is removed. A double-layered core remains.
↓
3. Core transcription: VP1 transcribes the negative strand to produce capped mRNAs.
↓
4. mRNA export: capped mRNAs enter the cytoplasm and serve as templates.
↓
5. Protein synthesis: structural proteins and viroplasm components are produced.
↓
6. Genome replication: mRNAs are copied into dsRNA genomes inside viroplasms, creating immature particles.
↓
7. ER budding: immature particles temporarily acquire a membrane.
↓
8. Maturation: the temporary membrane is lost and VP4 plus VP7 are added to form the mature outer capsid.
↓
9. Release: mature virions leave by cell lysis.
Two replication details marked in the lecture
Partial uncoating leaves a protected dual-layered core.
The immature particle temporarily acquires an ER membrane and then loses it before final outer-capsid assembly.

Rotavirus

The major Reoviridae pathogen in the lecture and a major cause of diarrheal illness in infants and young children.

Clinical importance and classification p. 14

  • Major cause of infantile gastroenteritis worldwide.
  • Other Reoviruses are described as less clinically important in humans.
  • Rotavirus also infects animals including calves, piglets, mice, and monkeys.
  • Groups A to E are listed with tentative F and G.
  • Group A is the most common human pathogen.
Antigen or proteinRole in lecture classification
VP6Group-specific antigen. Detected by ELISA and IEM.
VP4Neutralizing, type-specific antigen. Defines P type.
VP7Neutralizing, type-specific antigen. Defines G type.
  • Multiple serotypes have geographic variation and cross-species overlap.
  • Group A uses a dual serologic classification based on G and P types.
  • The lecture notes that genetic classification is beginning to replace serologic classification.

Pathogenesis p. 14

  • Rotavirus infects villus cells of the small intestine, not the stomach or colon.
  • It causes both malabsorption and secretory diarrhea.
Two core mechanisms
NSP4 is a viral enterotoxin that contributes to secretion.
Villus destruction leads to replacement by immature crypt cells that absorb poorly.
  • Up to 10¹² particles per gram of feces can be shed.
  • Shedding lasts about 2 to 12 days and can persist longer in malnourished patients.
  • Normal villi may require 3 to 8 weeks to recover.

Clinical features p. 14

  • Incubation: 1 to 3 days.
  • Watery diarrhea, vomiting, fever, abdominal pain, and dehydration.
  • Disease is more severe in infants and young children.
  • Adults often have mild or asymptomatic infection.
  • Group B rotavirus is associated with adult outbreaks in China in the lecture.
  • Immunodeficient children can have severe or prolonged disease.

Laboratory diagnosis p. 14 p. 15

  • Clinical findings cannot reliably distinguish Rotavirus from other diarrheal agents.
  • Stool collected early in illness is the lecture-marked specimen.
  • EIA is sensitive and detects the VP6 antigen in stool.
  • PCR is the most sensitive and specific and allows genotyping, but it is not routinely done because it is expensive.
  • Rapid immunochromatographic tests are point-of-care antigen tests that are easy to perform.

Epidemiology and immunity p. 15

  • Leading cause of gastroenteritis in children younger than 5 years in the lecture.
  • The lecture cites 3 to 5 billion cases annually worldwide and up to 1 million child deaths, especially in Africa, Asia, and Latin America.
  • Winter predominance.
  • Fecal-oral transmission. Nosocomial spread is common.
  • By age 3, about 90% of children are seropositive in the lecture.
  • Segment exchange among viruses in different hosts can produce new strains or genotypes.

Treatment and prevention p. 15

  • Treatment is supportive with oral or IV rehydration and electrolyte replacement.
  • Prevention uses sanitation and vaccination.
  • RotaShield, a rhesus-based vaccine from 1998, was withdrawn because of intussusception risk.
  • RotaTeq: live attenuated, oral pentavalent, human-bovine reassortant vaccine.
  • Rotarix: live attenuated, oral monovalent human vaccine.
  • The lecture states that current vaccines are safe and effective and that vaccination is the best control strategy worldwide.
ROTAvirus mnemonic
R = RNA virus, Reoviridae, dsRNA, segmented.
O = Oral-fecal spread and Oral vaccine.
T = Toxin NSP4, secretory diarrhea, and Tiny people or children.
A = Acute diarrhea in infants.

Caliciviridae and Norovirus

Small positive-sense RNA viruses with distinctive cup-shaped capsid morphology. Norovirus is the major epidemic gastroenteritis virus emphasized.

Caliciviridae structure and classification p. 15 p. 16

  • Key human members: Noroviruses, with Norwalk virus as prototype, and Sapoviruses, which include Sapporo-like viruses associated with childhood gastroenteritis.
  • Other genera listed are Nebovirus, Lagovirus, and Vesivirus, mainly affecting animals.
  • Small, non-enveloped, non-segmented positive-sense ssRNA viruses of about 27 to 40 nm.
  • The capsid has a single major structural protein, VP1.
  • Lecture-marked structural clue: cup-shaped morphology under electron microscopy.
  • Human Norovirus disease is associated with genogroups GI, GII, and GIV.
  • GII.4 strains are described as a major cause of worldwide outbreaks.

Norovirus pathogenesis and clinical features p. 16

  • Incubation: 24 to 48 hours.
  • Duration: 12 to 60 hours, usually self-limited.
  • Sudden-onset vomiting, watery diarrhea, low-grade fever, abdominal cramps, and malaise.
  • Main complication is dehydration, especially in young and elderly patients.
  • No chronic sequelae.
  • Viral shedding may continue for up to 1 month.

Epidemiology p. 16

Classic Norovirus clues
Most common cause of nonbacterial gastroenteritis worldwide in the lecture.
Highly infectious. As few as 10 particles can cause disease.
Classic settings: cruise ships, nursing homes, schools, and disaster shelters.
  • The lecture estimates 21 million cases annually in the United States.
  • Primary transmission is fecal-oral.
  • Foodborne transmission is important, especially through shellfish and contaminated food handlers.
  • Waterborne spread can occur through drinking or recreational water.
  • Person-to-person spread, fomites, and aerosolized vomitus are listed.
  • Virus can survive mild chlorine and heating to 60°C, and the lecture notes survival in steamed oysters.
  • The lecture compares this environmental stability to Hepatitis A.

Diagnosis, treatment, and prevention p. 16

Gold standard
RT-PCR is the gold standard for Norovirus.
Possible samples include stool, vomitus, food, and water.
The lecture notes that not all viruses can be diagnosed by cell culture, which is why RT-PCR is central here.
  • EM and IEM have limited use because sensitivity is low.
  • Serology by ELISA and IgG rise is mainly a research method.
  • Treatment is supportive with fluid and electrolyte replacement.
  • Prevention includes rigorous handwashing, proper food handling and cooking, isolation, disinfection of vomitus or stool contamination, and safe water supplies.
  • No vaccine is available in the lecture.
NORwalk mnemonic
N = Nausea and vomiting, sudden and severe.
O = Outbreaks on cruise ships, schools, and camps.
R = Rapid onset and recovery.
O = Oral-fecal transmission.

Cram Sheet

Fast final recall of lecture-marked must-knows, classic associations, core mechanisms, and differentiators.

Genome first

  • Picornaviridae → positive-sense ssRNA, nonsegmented, non-enveloped.
  • Reoviridae → dsRNA, segmented, non-enveloped. Segments permit reassortment and genetic shift.
  • Caliciviridae → positive-sense ssRNA, nonsegmented, non-enveloped, cup-shaped capsid depressions, major structural protein VP1.
  • Positive-sense RNA can be translated immediately. Negative-sense RNA must first be converted to positive-sense RNA.
  • Picornavirus nonsegmented RNA usually undergoes genetic drift, not genetic shift.

Picornavirus must-knows

  • Capsid proteins: VP1, VP2, VP3, VP4. VP1 to VP3 are surface. VP4 is internal.
  • The canyon is the receptor-binding site. Host-cell receptors can reach it while antibodies are excluded by its narrow shape in the lecture.
  • Replication is in the cytoplasm and is rapid at about 5 to 10 hours.
  • Receptors: Polio → PVR. Coxsackie B → CAR. Echovirus → DAF.
  • Most Enterovirus infections are asymptomatic.
  • Enterovirus recombination can occur when different strains co-infect one cell and the polymerase jumps between templates.
  • Enteroviruses are acid stable. Rhinoviruses are acid labile.

Poliovirus

  • Targets anterior horn motor neurons → asymmetric flaccid paralysis.
  • Flaccid = LMN → hypotonia and reduced or absent reflexes.
  • No sensory deficit.
  • Does not multiply in muscle. Muscle atrophy is secondary to denervation.
  • More than 90% of infections are asymptomatic.
  • Bulbar disease can injure motor pathways controlling breathing, swallowing, and airway protection.
  • Postpolio syndrome is late weakness from failure of compensatory axonal sprouts. Not viral reactivation.
  • Diagnosis: cell culture gold standard in the lecture. RT-PCR is rapid, sensitive, and specific. Stool gives the longest specimen yield.
  • Viral meningitis CSF: lymphocytic predominance, normal glucose, normal or increased protein.
  • IPV or Salk = killed, injected, no gut immunity.
  • OPV or Sabin = live attenuated, oral, adds gut IgA and can interrupt transmission, but has rare vaccine-derived or vaccine-associated risk.
  • Main difference: OPV induces gut immunity.

Coxsackievirus

  • Coxsackie A Triple H → Hand-foot-and-mouth disease, Herpangina, acute Hemorrhagic conjunctivitis.
  • Herpangina → posterior palate or pharyngeal vesicles and ulcers.
  • HFMD → oral lesions plus palms and soles. Vesicles heal without crusting.
  • Coxsackie A24 variant → acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis.
  • Coxsackie B → pleurodynia, myocarditis, severe neonatal systemic disease.
  • Lecture cue: A = Above the neck. B = Below the neck or Body organs.

Hepatitis A

  • Fecal-oral. Major sources: raw or undercooked shellfish, contaminated food, contaminated water.
  • HAV passes the stomach, reaches intestine, then replicates mainly in the liver, enters bile, and is excreted in stool.
  • Liver injury is immune-mediated. HAV is not usually directly cytopathic.
  • No chronic infection and no cirrhosis from HAV in the lecture.
  • IgM anti-HAV = acute infection. IgG anti-HAV with negative IgM = past infection or vaccination.
  • ELISA is the test of choice.
  • Post-exposure immunoglobulin should be given within 2 weeks when indicated.
  • Mnemonic anchors: A = Acute, A = Anus to mouth, HAV = Hand washing avoids virus.

Rotavirus

  • dsRNA + segmented + 11 segments + triple-layered capsid.
  • Groups listed: A to E, with tentative F and G. Human groups: A, B, C. Group A is most common.
  • VP6 = group antigen. VP4 = P type. VP7 = G type.
  • Partial uncoating leaves a protected double-layered core.
  • Immature particles temporarily acquire an ER membrane and then lose it.
  • Targets small-intestinal villus cells.
  • NSP4 enterotoxin → secretion. Villus destruction → immature crypt cells → poor absorption.
  • Symptoms: watery diarrhea, vomiting, fever, abdominal pain, dehydration.
  • Early stool specimen. EIA detects VP6. PCR is most sensitive and specific.
  • RotaShield was withdrawn for intussusception risk.
  • Current lecture vaccines: RotaTeq pentavalent and Rotarix monovalent, both oral live attenuated vaccines.
  • ROTA mnemonic: RNA Reoviridae, Oral-fecal and Oral vaccine, Toxin NSP4 and Tiny people, Acute infant diarrhea.

Norovirus

  • Most common cause of nonbacterial gastroenteritis worldwide in the lecture.
  • Very infectious. As few as 10 particles can cause disease.
  • Incubation 24 to 48 hours. Illness is brief and self-limited.
  • Sudden vomiting plus watery diarrhea.
  • Classic outbreak settings: cruise ships, nursing homes, schools, disaster shelters.
  • Spread: fecal-oral, food, water, person-to-person, fomites, and aerosolized vomitus.
  • RT-PCR = gold standard.
  • No vaccine in the lecture.
  • NORwalk: Nausea and vomiting, Outbreaks, Rapid onset and recovery, Oral-fecal.
